subject: english
name: Tenses
summary: Tense shows when an action happens: past, present or future. Each has four forms — simple, continuous, perfect and perfect continuous — built from the right helping verb and verb form.

topics.title: Present tenses
topics.summary: Simple present (habits, facts), present continuous (happening now), present perfect (just finished / result now), present perfect continuous (started in the past, still going).
topics.simple:
- **I play** — something you do regularly (simple present)
- **I am playing** — happening right now (present continuous)
- **I have played** — done, and it matters now (present perfect)
- **I have been playing** — started earlier and still going (present perfect continuous)
topics.explain:
**1. Simple present:** V1 (+ s/es with he, she, it)
- Use it for habits, facts and timetables: *She walks to school. Water boils at 100 °C. The train leaves at 6.*

**2. Present continuous:** am/is/are + V-ing
- Use it for actions happening now, or planned soon: *They are studying. I am meeting Riya tomorrow.*

**3. Present perfect:** has/have + V3 (past participle)
- Use it for actions completed recently, or whose result matters now: *I have finished my homework. She has lost her pen.*
- Don't use it with a finished past time like 'yesterday'.

**4. Present perfect continuous:** has/have been + V-ing
- Use it for an action that started in the past and is still continuing, often with **since** or **for**: *He has been reading since 5 o'clock. We have been waiting for an hour.*
topics.example: Wrong: *I have seen him yesterday.* Right: *I saw him yesterday.* 'Yesterday' is a finished time, so use the simple past, not the present perfect.
keyPoints: Present perfect: has/have + V3 — completed, result now
Present perfect continuous: has/have been + V-ing — since/for
Since + point of time (since Monday); for + length of time (for 2 hours)

topics.title: Past tenses
topics.summary: Simple past (finished action), past continuous (in progress in the past), past perfect (the earlier of two past actions), past perfect continuous (continuing up to a point in the past).
topics.simple:
- **I played** — finished in the past
- **I was playing** — in progress at a past moment
- **I had played** — happened before another past action
- **I had been playing** — going on for a while before a past moment
topics.explain:
**1. Simple past:** V2
- A completed action at a definite past time: *We visited Jaipur last year.*

**2. Past continuous:** was/were + V-ing
- An action in progress at a past time, often interrupted: *I was reading when the lights went out.*

**3. Past perfect:** had + V3
- The **earlier** of two past actions: *The train had left before we reached the station.*

**4. Past perfect continuous:** had been + V-ing
- An action continuing for some time before another past point: *She had been practising for months before the competition.*
topics.example: *When I reached the hall, the show had started.* The show started first (past perfect: had started), then I reached (simple past: reached).
keyPoints: Past continuous: was/were + V-ing — in progress
Past perfect: had + V3 — earlier of two past actions
Past perfect continuous: had been + V-ing

topics.title: Future tenses
topics.summary: Simple future (will + V1), future continuous (will be + V-ing), future perfect (will have + V3), future perfect continuous (will have been + V-ing).
topics.simple:
- **I will play** — later
- **I will be playing** — in progress at a future moment
- **I will have played** — finished before a future time
- **I will have been playing** — going on for a while until a future time
topics.explain:
**1. Simple future:** will + V1
- *I will call you tonight.* ('Going to' + V1 is also used for plans: *I am going to study.*)

**2. Future continuous:** will be + V-ing
- *At 8 pm tomorrow, I will be travelling.*

**3. Future perfect:** will have + V3
- *By next week, she will have finished the project.*

**4. Future perfect continuous:** will have been + V-ing
- *By June, he will have been working here for two years.*
topics.example: *By the time you arrive, I will have cooked dinner.* The cooking will be complete before your arrival — future perfect.
keyPoints: Future perfect: will have + V3 (by + time)
Future perfect continuous: will have been + V-ing

keyConcepts.meaning: Base form, past form and past participle of a verb, e.g. go–went–gone, write–wrote–written.
'Since' takes a point of time (since 2020); 'for' takes a length of time (for three years).
had + V3; used for the earlier of two actions in the past.

formulas: Present: V1 · am/is/are + V-ing · has/have + V3 · has/have been + V-ing
Past: V2 · was/were + V-ing · had + V3 · had been + V-ing
Future: will + V1 · will be + V-ing · will have + V3 · will have been + V-ing
commonMistakes: Using the present perfect with past time words: 'I have seen him yesterday' ✗ → 'I saw him yesterday' ✓.
Mixing up since and for: 'since two hours' ✗ → 'for two hours' ✓.
Forgetting -s with he/she/it in the simple present: 'She play' ✗ → 'She plays' ✓.
Using V2 after 'did': 'Did you went?' ✗ → 'Did you go?' ✓.
revision: Simple present for habits and facts; add -s/-es with he/she/it.
Continuous = be + V-ing; perfect = have/has/had/will have + V3.
Present perfect: not with 'yesterday', 'last year' or 'ago'.
Past perfect = the earlier of two past actions.
Since + point of time; for + length of time.

faqs.q: What is the difference between since and for?
faqs.a: Use **since** with a point in time (since Monday, since 2019, since morning). Use **for** with a length of time (for two days, for an hour, for years). Example: *I have lived here since 2020* / *for five years*.

faqs.q: When do we use the past perfect tense?
faqs.a: Use the **past perfect (had + V3)** for the action that happened first when you talk about two past actions. *The film had started when we reached.* — the film started first.

faqs.q: Why is 'I have seen him yesterday' wrong?
faqs.a: The present perfect (have seen) can't be used with a finished past time like 'yesterday'. Use the simple past: *I saw him yesterday.*

faqs.q: What is the difference between simple past and present perfect?
faqs.a: The **simple past** (I finished) is for an action at a definite, finished time in the past. The **present perfect** (I have finished) connects the past to now — the time isn't stated, or the result matters now.

quiz.q: Look! The children ___ in the rain.
quiz.explain: 'Look!' shows it's happening now — present continuous.
'Yesterday' is a finished past time — simple past.

quiz.q: The train ___ before we reached the station.
quiz.explain: The earlier of two past actions takes the past perfect.
2019 is a point in time → since.

quiz.q: By next Monday, I ___ the book.
I ___ TV when my mother called.
quiz.explain: An action in progress that was interrupted → past continuous.

quiz.q: At 9 pm tonight, I ___ my exam notes.
quiz.explain: In progress at a future moment → future continuous.

quiz.q: They ___ for two hours when the rain stopped.
quiz.explain: Continuing for a time before a past moment → past perfect continuous.
